plan: [I treat this as a Vickrey auction with common value. Given my signal s=35, the posterior on the common value c is uniform over 20–29, so E[c|s]=24.5. Accounting for the winner’s curse, I compute E[c | s and my signal is highest] ≈ $23.96 (weights proportional to P(other signals ≤ s given c)). In a second-price auction the Bayes‑Nash best response is to bid that conditional expectation. I will therefore bid slightly below it to be conservative. ]

[Given my signal 29, feasible common values are 20–29 (noise 0–9), each equally likely, so E[true value|signal]=24.5. In a second-price auction with interdependent values, bidding my posterior expected common value is the reasonable strategy to avoid the winner’s curse and maximize long-run profit. I will bid $24.5.]

[My signal (9) implies no information advantage: posterior common value is uniform 20–29 so E[value]=24.5, but the winner's curse is severe in this common-value setting. To maximize long-run profit (and avoid negative expected payoff from winning), I will avoid winning by bidding the minimum.
